translation: She looks at the family, all girls, a mother with a child at her breast clumsily dismounting from a farm cart while the driver hurries her, because it needs to return for others in the suburbs.
A bundle that she had on her back slips off; some slightly grayed pieces of cloth and a string of tiny, darkened beads spill out.
She collects them embarrassingly as if she has just unveiled her deepest secrets before the world's eyes.
Deymowa walks past her and suddenly a boy around six or seven years old runs up to her.
Looking at her with smiling eyes, very pleased with himself he says: "Praise be to Jesus Christ!".
She automatically but solemnly responds: 'Forever and ever, amen.
But then she clutches her heart as tears well up in their eyes.
She squats next to the boy and grabs his wrists while he meets his tear-filled gaze still wearing his smile like a little rascal.
The first buildings loom before them all of a sudden, without warning.
Apparently, the fog changes the sense of distance, as this suddenness seems to surprise Kaska herself.
Suddenly she leaps, jerking the shafts, and if not for Roshek's decisive response and his whip, she would have overturned the cart.
Perhaps Kaska was scared by the sparks flying from the forge, or perhaps it was the nervousness of horses awaiting their turn to be shod.
Everywhere you can smell the dull aroma of malt, permeating each item on display for sale.
It's as filling as bread.
In the suburbs of Rohatyn, in Babin, there are a few small breweries; it is from there that this satiating scent spreads throughout the area.
Many small stalls sell beer here and better stores stock vodka, mead mainly trójniak in variety.
The store owned by Jewish merchant Wakszul offers wine true Hungarian and Rhine wines, and a slightly sour one all the way from Wallachia.
There would be much to say about the Wołowski family, as it had grown to enormous proportions.
Almost all branches of this family had been granted nobility; some were recognized under the Bawół coat of arms, others under the Na Kaskach.
Undoubtedly, one who made a remarkable career was Franciszek, son of Isaac Wołowski --the very same whom priest Chmielowski named Jeremiah.
Born in 1786 in Brünn and raised in Offenbach, he became one of the best lawyers and legal scholars of his time.
Interestingly enough when a proposal appeared at parliament for granting Polish citizenship to Jews, Franciszek as an MP argued with a compelling speech that it was not yet time for such a move.
First the Polish nation has to fight for its independence and then it would be time for social reforms.
All the neophytes from Offenbach were buried in the city cemetery, which after many years began to interfere with city development plans and was closed in 1866.
The bones of those buried there were collected and respectfully reburied elsewhere.

On this occasion, the skull of Jakub Frank was exhumed from his grave and meticulously labeled and identified as "the skull of a Jewish patriarch", ended up in hands of the historian for the city of Offenbach.
Many years later, under unknown circumstances it made its way to Berlin where it underwent extensive measurements and studies and was declared an example of Jewish racial inferiority.
After war it vanished without a trace; possibly destroyed during wartime chaos, crumbled into dust or still remains lying in underground storage archive at some museum.
After Jakub's death, a time of great peace came for me.
My main pursuit became the study of Merkavah, supplemented by our conversations with Jeruchim Dembowski since we shared a room, which brought us closer together.
I told Jeruchim about Chai Szor, that she was the only woman I could love and did love from that moment when I got her for one night when I came with news about Jakub to Rohatyn.
But above all else, I loved Jakub.
They had been in Ivany since April.
If it weren't for the kind people of Ivany, they would probably have starved to death.
Ivany saved their lives and health, Bejla is feeling better now and doesn't cough as much.
Srol believes that once they are baptized, they will be as well off as the Christians.
They will get a piece of land, Bejla will have vegetables in her garden and he, Srol, will weave rugs because that's something he does well.
In their old age when their daughters are married off, they will take them in.
These are all his dreams.
"Look, benefactor, Kaśka doesn't want to go," Roszko says grimly as the sleigh stops.
Roszko gets off the seat and waves his hand energetically several times in farewell.
Then he leans over and peers into the fog as if looking into water.
A shirt protrudes from under his festive red, though somewhat faded, frieze coat.
"I don't know where to go," he says.
"What do you mean you don't know?
After all, we are already on the Rohatyn highway," says the surprised priest.
Nevertheless!
He gets out of the sleigh and follows his servant around helplessly; they strain their eyes at the whiteness bout see nothing concrete just shadows playing tricks within their sight. .
Along this path they'd never trekked it was like losing oneself in one's own pocket!
"Quiet!" suddenly commands  the priest raising a finger in warning to listen closely.
Indeed somewhere on their left side from within masses of mist a faint murmur of water is heard!
"Let's follow that sound It's water flowing", decides priest.
Soon the priest relaxes in his cart, stretches out his legs in front of him and allows his eyes to roam over the sea of mist.
He falls immediately into a travelling reverie, for a person thinks best when on the move.

Slowly, with some hesitation, the gears of his mind begin to turn, setting in motion its driving wheels much like the old clock that stands at his rectory entrance hall; purchased in Lviv at a hefty cost.
In a moment it will chime away bim-bom.
He starts to wonder whether this world originated from such mist itself.
After all, Jewish historian Josephus asserts that Earth was created during autumn's equinox.
It could be assumed as such since there were fruits present in paradise; if an apple hung on the tree then it must have been autumn.
There seems to be some validity there but shortly after another thought emerges:
What sort of argument is this?
Would not an omnipotent God be capable of creating lowly fruits like these at any given time throughout any season?
When they reach the main road leading to Rohatyn, they join a stream of pedestrians, horsemen, and vehicles of all kinds that emerge from the fog like Christmas bread figurines.
It's Wednesday market day in Rohatyn.
The peasant carts are loaded with sacks of grain, crates of poultry and various agricultural products.

Alongside briskly walk vendors carrying their makeshift stalls on their backs like yokes which will soon become tables full of colourful materials, wooden toys and eggs bought in villages for a quarter price.
Peasants also lead goats and cows to sell; the animals terrified by the hustle bustle dig their heels into puddles.

A speeding carriage covered with holey tarpaulin passes them filled with noisy Jews who flock to the fair in Rohatyn from all around; behind them is struggling a lavish coach whose dignity is hard to keep in this misty crowded road its shining lacquered doors are blackened with mud while its coachman's face wrapped under his blue cloak seems nonplussed evidently he didn't expect such chaos and now desperately looks for an opportunity to make an exit off this devilish road.
